Sunday, 4 October 2026:

\- Race: P17, 55 laps

- The Bahrain GP was tough with Carlos Sainz, who finished the race in seventeenth place despite the fact that he had climbed up to the points at one stage.
- Carlos took the right decision to start the race on Intermediate tyres, which allowed him to move from thirteenth on the starting grid all the way to sixth, with a big margin over the following cars.
- A crash by Valtteri Bottas led to a Safety-Car, which brought the group together. This, combined with a slow pit-stop, meant Carlos was down to seventh.
- At the restart, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto crashed into Carlos’ Williams. He then fell to the bottom of the standings, away from the points.

**QUOTES:**

“ _We did everything right at the start of the race and managed to climb all the way to P6. Unfortunately, after getting hit at the first restart I dropped quickly down the order and it was very tough for us to recover. We knew we would struggle with pace today and scoring points was always going to be difficult, but we need to look into the execution and make sure we have a better weekend next week in Singapore. We’ll try to bounce back and keep pushing_”.

**COMING UP:**

Singapore GP, Marina Bay Street Circuit – 9-11 October 2026

Open Extended Reactions

"Horrible," "sad," and "totally unacceptable" were among the reactions of Formula 1's drivers to the sport's attempt at racing in wet conditions at Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

A deluge of rain as the cars arrived on the grid resulted in the start of the race being delayed by 40 minutes before the first attempt was made to get racing underway behind a safety car.

But before the cars could complete a single lap behind the safety car, a bug in the software supplied to all teams by the FIA resulted in multiple drivers losing power and dropping down the order.

Initially [Max Verstappen](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4665), who was set to start from pole position, lost power, before [Lewis Hamilton](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=868), who was alongside him on the front row of the grid, ground to a halt and had to restart his Ferrari's power unit on the pit straight.

The FIA later said that "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars."

But several drivers chose to sum up the situation more concisely, pointing the finger squarely at this year's complicated power unit regulations.

"\[It was\] horrible," reigning champion [Lando Norris](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5579) said. "It proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff on the electronic side."

When the issue became apparent, all cars were told to return to the pits, where a software patch was supplied by the FIA and uploaded by each team.

The resulting delay meant the start of the race was over 90 minutes behind schedule.

"We missed some good racing, wet tires at the beginning, we should have been out there running," Aston Martin driver [Lance Stroll](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4775) said. "Instead cars are fixing their software issues. It's a bit sad to see."

Cadillac driver [Sergio Pérez](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4472) added: "I mean, it's obviously not great what happened today -- I'm sure we will learn from it as a sport, but what happened today is totally unacceptable for the sport."

\- **[Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires](https://www.espn.co.uk/f1/story/_/id/50074959/max-verstappen-wins-pole-kimi-antonelli-extends-title-lead-sepang-formula-1-bahrain-gp-malaysia)**

\- **[Bahrain GP in Malaysia: George Russell suffers major title blow after race retirement](https://www.espn.co.uk/f1/story/_/id/50074961/bahrain-gp-george-russell-malaysia-sepang-formula-1)**

\- **[George Russell on Bahrain GP retirement: 'Beyond disappointment' as title chances all but over](https://www.espn.co.uk/f1/story/_/id/50074962/george-russell-bahrain-gp-retirement-disappointment-title-chances-all-sepang-formula-1)**

For many drivers, it was further proof that this year's regulations, which were designed so that nearly 50% of the car's power comes from its battery, are overcomplicated.

"That's the problem that we have, these engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented," race winner Verstappen said. "When there is some kind of error or glitch, or whatever you want to call it, that's the problem.

"I triggered it first, then I look in my mirror, and I just see everyone ... I was like, wait, are they waiting for me or?"

Hamilton, who finished third, likened the situation to Lego's marketing stunt at the British Grand Prix, where all the drivers were given electric go-karts to race against each other.

"It was like the Lego race!" Hamilton said while sitting next to Verstappen at the postrace news conference.

"Yeah, we had the same speed," Verstappen responded.

[Kimi Antonelli](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5829), who finished second in Sunday's race, chimed in: "It was insane. Like at some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Williams driver [Carlos Sainz](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=4686) called on the sport to "have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation."

"It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the \[power units\], for the manufacturers. It is too complicated," he said. "Again, my only question mark is who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go? We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong. ...

"Not a lot more to say -- just learn as a sport not to do those mistakes again and not suffer from the same strange cases."

Once racing got underway, the track dried up and the grand prix featured two further safety car periods to clear cars that retired from the race in dangerous locations.

[George Russell](http://www.espn.com/rpm/driver?seriesId=6&driverId=5503), who retired with a power unit issue under the final safety car period, said the fans that turned up to Malaysia's first grand prix since 2017 deserved a better show.

"The whole day felt like a bit of a faff, with the delay and then the red flag and then endless laps under the safety car and then suddenly doing extra laps to allow \[Sergio Pérez\] to overtake \[behind the safety car\], it didn't feel very F1 today," he said.

"I'd have been a bit disappointed if I was in the stands, watching that unfold, so ... that wasn't good."

The Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia has been red-flagged after several cars suffered power unit gremlins during a wet set of formation laps.

After a heavy tropical thunderstorm, the action at Malaysian Sepang was set to get underway with a number of laps behind the safety car followed by a standing start.

But ahead of F1's first-ever wet event under the 2026 regulations, a number of cars suffered power unit gremlins in the rain, suspected to be software-related.

Initially, polesitter Max Verstappen reported a lack of acceleration from his Red Bull before the Dutchman got going again. Soon after, second-placed Lewis Hamilton reported a similar issue on his Ferrari, with the Briton crawling around the first formation lap as the rest of the field passed him. One lap later, Hamilton too managed to get going again.

More cars, including Racing Bulls man Liam Lawson, Audi driver Gabriel Bortoleto and Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas, also appeared to struggle with similar problems, with race control suspending the start procedure and throwing a red flag.
